Overview

Introduction

Erythemato-squamous diseases present one of dermatology's most persistent diagnostic challenges — six conditions that look nearly identical, yet require entirely different treatments.

6Disease Classes
366Patients
34Features
95%+ML Target

Erythemato-squamous diseases are a group of inflammatory skin conditions that share a frustratingly similar clinical appearance — redness (erythema) and scaling — yet represent fundamentally different pathologies. The six conditions studied here are psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, lichen planus, pityriasis rosea, chronic dermatitis, and pityriasis rubra pilaris. In day-to-day clinical practice, patients present with lesions that look nearly indistinguishable even under microscopic examination, leading to prolonged and sometimes incorrect treatment courses that significantly affect quality of life.

Accurate diagnosis has historically required a combination of clinical evaluation and invasive skin biopsy — procedures that are uncomfortable, expensive, and slow. Papulosquamous disorders alone account for a meaningful percentage of all outpatient dermatology visits worldwide, with psoriasis affecting an estimated 2–3% of the global population. The sheer burden of these conditions makes efficient, non-invasive diagnostic tools a genuine public health priority.

This project applies the data science lifecycle to a structured dataset of 366 patients, each described by 34 clinical and histopathological features. By combining dimensionality reduction (PCA), unsupervised clustering, and association rule mining, the aim is to uncover the hidden structure in this data — identifying which feature combinations reliably distinguish disease classes, and whether machine-discovered groupings correspond to known medical diagnoses. Recent hybrid deep learning approaches on this dataset have achieved classification accuracy above 95%, reinforcing the potential of computational tools to meaningfully assist clinical decision-making.

The transition from Module 2's unsupervised explorations to Module 3's supervised learning represents a fundamental shift in our methodology. While clustering and association rule mining revealed hidden structure without labels, supervised learning leverages the known disease diagnoses to train predictive models. Three complementary paradigms are brought to bear: Naïve Bayes captures probabilistic relationships between symptoms and diagnosis; Decision Trees learn explicit if–then rules that mirror clinical reasoning; and Logistic Regression provides a probabilistic linear boundary between classes. Together, these approaches answer a question with direct clinical utility — given a new patient's feature profile, which of the six erythemato-squamous diseases is most likely?

The stakes of accurate classification here are not abstract. Misdiagnosing psoriasis as lichen planus, for instance, leads to fundamentally different treatment regimens — one managed with biologics, the other with corticosteroids — with real consequences for patient outcomes. Machine learning models trained on well-curated histopathological and clinical data can serve as a decision-support layer, flagging atypical presentations and confirming tentative diagnoses. The goal of this module is therefore not merely academic performance metrics, but a demonstration that data science can meaningfully augment dermatological practice, particularly in resource-constrained settings where specialist access is limited.

Figure 1 — Clinical presentation of psoriasis

Well-defined erythematous plaques with characteristic silvery-white scale — the most prevalent disease class in this dataset (112 of 366 patients). Defined borders and scattered distribution are key clinical identifiers.

Figure 2 — Histopathological cross-section (psoriasis)

Key tissue features: acanthosis (thickened epidermis), parakeratosis (nucleated cells in scale), elongated and clubbed rete ridges, thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis, and inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis — the most discriminating variables across all six disease classes.

Research Questions

Ten questions guide this project from raw data to actionable findings:

Which features most strongly differentiate psoriasis from other classes?
How does age affect the severity of erythema and scaling?
Are there correlations between histopathological and clinical features?
Can family history predict disease class?
Which features are most important for early detection?
Do specific features cluster together for certain disease types?
How balanced are the classes — do we need resampling methods?
Can dimensionality reduction improve model performance?
Are there age or gender biases in the dataset?
How well do models generalise to previously unseen patient data?

Module 1 · Exploration

Exploratory Data Analysis

Ten visualisations that surface the structure, distributions, and relationships within the dataset before any modelling is applied.

Class Distribution

This bar chart shows how patient cases are distributed across the six erythemato-squamous diseases in the dataset. Disease class 1 has the highest number of samples, while class 6 has the fewest, indicating that the dataset is imbalanced. Such imbalance is important because machine learning models may become biased toward more frequent classes, potentially reducing performance for rare conditions. The variation in class frequencies also reflects real-world clinical scenarios where certain skin diseases are more commonly diagnosed than others. Understanding this distribution helps guide decisions such as applying class weighting or resampling techniques to ensure fair model performance across all disease types.

Age Distribution

The histogram illustrates the age distribution of patients included in the dermatology dataset. Most patients fall between approximately 20 and 50 years, with fewer cases at very young and older ages. The smooth curve indicates a fairly continuous distribution rather than isolated age clusters, suggesting that erythemato-squamous diseases affect a broad age range. Age can play a role in disease manifestation and diagnosis, so recognizing its distribution helps assess whether age should be treated as an influential predictive feature. Since the data does not show extreme skewness, age appears well represented and suitable for use in classification modeling.

Erythema by Class

The provided box plot illustrates the distribution of Erythema Scores (ranging from approximately 0.5 to 3.0) across six distinct Disease Classes. Disease Classes 1 and 2 show the highest central tendencies, with medians and upper quartiles reaching the maximum score of 3.0, though Class 1 exhibits a much broader range of lower scores. In contrast, Classes 3, 4, and 6 appear highly concentrated, with their primary data clusters flattened around a score of 2.0, punctuated only by specific outliers at the 1.0 and 3.0 marks. Class 5 displays a unique downward shift compared to the first two categories, with its interquartile range spanning between 1.0 and 2.0, suggesting that while redness is present, it is generally less severe in this group than in Classes 1 and 2.

Correlation Heatmap

The provided Correlation Heatmap illustrates the linear relationships between various clinical and histopathological features, with a color scale ranging from strong negative correlation (deep blue, -0.6) to strong positive correlation (deep red, 1.0). A prominent cluster of high positive correlation is visible among features like clubbing_rete_ridges, elongation_rete_ridges, and thinning_suprapapillary_epidermis, suggesting these structural changes often occur simultaneously in certain skin conditions. Additionally, polygonal_papules shows a strong positive relationship with oral_mucosal_involvement, melanin_incontinence, and focal_hypergranulosis, which may indicate a specific diagnostic pattern. Conversely, the class variable exhibits several negative correlations, particularly with erythema and scaling, implying that as these specific symptom scores increase, the numerical value of the disease classification tends to decrease.

Pairwise Relationships

This Pairwise Relationship plot (or pair plot) visualizes the interactions between clinical features—erythema, scaling, acanthosis, and age— color-coded by the six disease classes. The diagonal density plots reveal that while most classes share overlapping distributions for physical symptoms, Class 6 (yellow) stands out with a significantly younger age distribution compared to the other groups, which peak more broadly between ages 30 and 50. The scatter plots indicate that the clinical scores (erythema, scaling, and acanthosis) are categorical in nature, as data points are clustered at integer values (0, 1, 2, and 3), showing that high scores in these categories are common across several diseases but appear most densely populated for Class 1 (red). Overall, while physical symptoms show significant overlap, age appears to be a stronger differentiator for identifying specific classes like Class 6.

Family History

This grouped bar chart displays the distribution of Family History across the six disease classes, where 0 signifies no history and 1 signifies a positive history. Across all classes, the vast majority of patients do not have a family history of their respective conditions, with Class 1 showing the highest count in this category at 80 patients. Interestingly, Class 1 and Class 6 appear most distinct regarding genetic prevalence; Class 1 has a significant secondary cluster of over 30 patients with a positive family history, while Class 6 shows an equal split of 10 patients with and 10 without a family history. Conversely, Classes 2, 3, 4, and 5 show very few to no instances of positive family history, suggesting that these specific conditions may be less driven by hereditary factors compared to Class 1.

Age Distribution per Class

The provided box plot illustrates the Age Distribution Across Disease Classes, highlighting significant demographic differences between the various conditions. Most disease classes (1 through 5) exhibit broad age ranges, typically spanning from approximately 10 to 70 years, with median ages clustering between 35 and 40. Disease Class 6 stands out as a clear outlier in this dataset, presenting a much younger and more concentrated patient profile with a median age below 10 and a maximum age (excluding one outlier) reaching only about 16. This stark contrast is corroborated by the pairwise density plots, which show Class 6 (yellow) having a sharp, narrow peak at the lower end of the age scale while other classes show wider, overlapping curves. Such a distinct age distribution for Class 6 suggests it may represent a pediatric-specific condition, whereas the other classes are prevalent across a wider adult demographic.

Acanthosis by Class

The Distribution of Acanthosis by Disease Class violin plot illustrates the density and spread of acanthosis scores across the six clinical categories. Most classes exhibit a high density around a score of 2.0, with Class 3 and Class 5 showing more prominent clusters at the higher end of the scale, near 3.0. In contrast, Class 4 displays a noticeable bimodal-like shape with a significant concentration of lower scores near 1.0, suggesting a generally less severe presentation of acanthosis compared to the other groups. This variation aligns with the Pairwise Relationship data, which shows that while acanthosis scores are categorical (0–3), their frequency and intensity fluctuate depending on the specific disease class being observed.

Feature Correlation with Class

The Correlation of Features with Disease Class heatmap provides a detailed look at which clinical and histopathological markers most strongly influence the numerical classification of the skin conditions in this dataset. According to the chart, the features with the strongest positive correlations to higher class numbers are fibrosis_papillary_dermis (0.53), follicular_papules (0.48), and perifollicular_parakeratosis (0.46), suggesting these specific markers are highly characteristic of the upper disease classes. Conversely, several features show strong negative correlations with the class variable, most notably thinning_suprapapillary_epidermis (-0.68) and clubbing_rete_ridges (-0.67), which indicates that as these symptoms become more severe, the disease is more likely to be categorized into the lower numerical classes, such as Class 1 or 2. This aligns with other visual data, such as the Pairwise Relationship plot, where Class 1 (red) and Class 2 (blue) show dense clusters for symptoms like erythema and scaling, which also carry negative correlation coefficients of -0.34 and -0.47 respectively. Additionally, while age shows a negative correlation of -0.25 with the class variable, the Age Distribution box plot clarifies that this is largely driven by the extremely young demographic of Class 6, which has a median age below 10, whereas the other classes are distributed broadly across adult ages. Ultimately, the heatmap clarifies that while many features like focal_hypergranulosis (0.063) or itching (0.055) have negligible direct impact on the class number, structural histopathological changes like PNL_infiltrate (-0.55) and scalp_involvement (-0.53) serve as the most significant mathematical differentiators for identifying the specific disease category.

Erythema vs Scaling

This scatter plot examines the relationship between Erythema Score and Scaling Score, categorized by the six disease classes. Because both metrics use a discrete scoring system (typically 0–3), the data points are strictly aligned on a grid, showing that Class 1 (blue) is the most widespread, appearing at almost every combination of high erythema and high scaling scores. Class 2 (orange) and Class 3 (green) show more specific clusters; for instance, Class 2 is notably present at the intersection of a 2.0 erythema score and 2.0 scaling score, while Class 3 appears at lower levels of both. Class 5 (purple) is concentrated at lower scaling scores (0.0 to 1.0) even when erythema scores are present, which aligns with the Correlation Heatmap where scaling has a negative correlation with higher class numbers. Notably, Class 6 (brown) and Class 4 (red) are less visible or overlapping in this specific view, suggesting that these two symptoms alone may not be the primary clinical differentiators for those conditions compared to features like Age or Family History.

Module 2 · Dimensionality Reduction

Principal Component Analysis

PCA transforms 34 correlated features into a smaller set of uncorrelated axes that capture the most variance — making the invisible structure of high-dimensional clinical data visible.

What is PCA?

Principal Component Analysis is an unsupervised technique that reorients a dataset along the directions of greatest variance. It computes the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix — each eigenvector defines a new axis called a principal component (PC). The corresponding eigenvalue measures how much variance that axis captures. Projecting data onto the top-k PCs achieves several things at once: noise reduction, elimination of multicollinearity, faster downstream computation, and the ability to visualise hundreds of features in just two or three dimensions. Patients that are clinically similar will appear geometrically close in PCA space.

Data & Preparation

The cleaned dataset (df_saved.csv, 366 × 35) was used. The class column was removed — PCA is applied to features only. All 34 remaining features are ordinal numeric; no additional encoding was needed. Data was then normalised with StandardScaler before any PCA was applied.

01
Load & separate labels
df_saved.csv → save class labels → drop 'class' → X (366 × 34)
02
Normalise with StandardScaler
Each feature centred to mean = 0, scaled to std = 1. Prevents wide-range features from dominating principal components.
03
PCA with n_components = 2
Project onto top 2 PCs → 2D scatter coloured by disease class. Measure cumulative variance.
04
PCA with n_components = 3
Project onto top 3 PCs → 3D scatter. Compare retained variance to 2D result.
05
Full PCA — variance analysis
Run PCA over all 34 components. Plot scree + cumulative variance curve. Determine minimum n for ≥ 95% retention.
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.decomposition import PCA scaler = StandardScaler() X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X) # mean=0, std=1 per feature pca2 = PCA(n_components=2) X_pca2 = pca2.fit_transform(X_scaled) pca3 = PCA(n_components=3) X_pca3 = pca3.fit_transform(X_scaled) pca_full = PCA() # retain all components pca_full.fit(X_scaled)

Module 2 · Unsupervised Learning

Clustering Analysis

Three fundamentally different clustering paradigms are applied to the same data, revealing how much of the known disease structure can be recovered without any diagnostic labels.

Comparing the Three Methods

MethodCore approachRequires k?Handles noise?Cluster shape
K-Means Minimises within-cluster variance; iteratively reassigns points to nearest centroid Yes — must specify in advance No — every point assigned Globular / convex
Hierarchical (Ward) Builds a dendrogram by greedily merging the pair that minimises variance increase at each step No — cut the tree at any level No — every point assigned Globular (Ward linkage)
DBSCAN Connects core points within ε-radius; expands clusters through density; sparse points become noise No — discovered automatically Yes — flags outliers explicitly Arbitrary shape

Data Preparation

The 3D PCA-reduced, StandardScaler-normalised, label-free data from the previous section is used as input for all three algorithms. Reducing to 3 dimensions removes noise, decorrelates features, and makes every distance-based method more reliable.

01
Remove label column
True class labels saved separately for post-hoc comparison only — not used during clustering
02
StandardScaler normalisation
Mean = 0, Std = 1 per feature — distance metrics are scale-sensitive
03
PCA reduction to 3 dimensions
~60% variance retained; noise suppressed; enables visual validation of clustering results

K-Means — Silhouette Method

Rather than guessing k, the Silhouette Score was computed for k = 2 through k = 11. The score measures how similar each point is to its own cluster vs. the nearest other cluster (range −1 to +1; higher is better). The three k values with the highest scores were selected for detailed analysis.

Figure 9 — Silhouette Score by k

The three best k values are marked with dashed lines. The optimal k balances cluster compactness with clinical interpretability.

Figure 10 — K-Means with Three Best k Values

One scatter per selected k, projected onto PC1–PC2. Black stars (★) mark cluster centroids. Colours indicate assigned cluster, not true disease class.

Figure 11 — Discovered Clusters vs True Disease Classes

Left: true diagnostic labels. Right: best K-Means result. The alignment reveals how much of the disease structure is geometrically recoverable without supervision.

Interpretation: K-Means with k = 6 shows the strongest alignment with true classes. Class 6 and Class 1 cluster distinctly. Classes 2 and 4 overlap — mirroring the genuine diagnostic difficulty clinicians experience with these conditions in practice.

Hierarchical Clustering — Dendrogram

Ward linkage agglomerative clustering was applied to the 3D PCA data. Ward's method minimises total within-cluster variance at every merge, making it the most comparable to K-Means in terms of cluster geometry while providing a richer hierarchical picture.

Figure 12 — Ward Linkage Dendrogram (truncated to last 30 merges)

The red dashed line marks a natural cut point. The number of branches below the cut corresponds to the discovered groups. The vertical heights of merges indicate cluster dissimilarity.

Figure 13 — Agglomerative Clustering (k = 6) in PCA Space

Cluster assignments mapped to 2D PCA coordinates for direct visual comparison with K-Means output.

Comparison with K-Means: The dendrogram suggests 5–7 natural groupings, consistent with the 6 known disease classes. Hierarchical and K-Means produce similar major groupings; differences concentrate at the boundaries between overlapping middle classes.

DBSCAN

DBSCAN (eps = 1.2, min_samples = 5) identifies regions of high density as clusters and marks low-density patients as noise. Unlike K-Means and hierarchical methods, it does not force every patient into a group.

Figure 14 — DBSCAN Clustering Results

Grey × marks indicate noise — patients whose feature profiles are insufficiently similar to any dense cluster. These are likely atypical presentations or borderline diagnostic cases.

Interpretation: DBSCAN recovers 3–5 core dense regions, corresponding to the most clinically distinct diseases. The confirmed noise points are a clinically meaningful finding — DBSCAN is the only method to flag patients who may not fit cleanly into any single category, which directly mirrors real diagnostic uncertainty.

Conclusions

All three methods consistently identify Class 6 (Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris) as the most distinct group and Class 1 (Psoriasis) as a dense, separable cluster. The methods diverge most on Classes 2, 4, and 5 — whose overlapping clinical presentations make them genuinely difficult to separate, computationally as well as clinically. The consistency of this finding across three entirely different algorithmic approaches gives it strong credibility.

Module 2 · Association Rule Mining

Association Rule Mining

ARM asks a different question from clustering: not how are patients grouped, but which symptoms reliably appear together — discovering co-occurrence patterns that characterise conditions without any disease labels.

(a) Overview

Association Rule Mining discovers if–then relationships in transactional data. A rule takes the form {A} → {B}: when a patient shows symptom A, symptom B is also likely present. Rules are evaluated using three measures:

MeasureFormulaWhat it means
Support P(A ∪ B) How common is this pattern? Fraction of all patients showing both symptoms.
Confidence P(B | A) = support(A∪B) / support(A) Given A is present, how reliably does B appear? Range: 0–1.
Lift confidence(A→B) / support(B) How much more likely is B given A vs. chance? Lift > 1 means genuine positive association.

The Apriori algorithm finds all frequent itemsets — feature combinations appearing in at least min_support fraction of patients — using the Apriori principle to prune the search space efficiently: any subset of a frequent itemset must also be frequent, so infrequent supersets are discarded early. Rules are then generated from those itemsets that meet a minimum confidence threshold.

Figure 15

A rule {A,B}→{C} extracted from a transaction pool. Support measures how often the full pattern appears; confidence measures reliability given the antecedent; lift measures how far above chance the association is.

Figure 16

The Apriori algorithm builds candidate itemsets level by level. Any superset of an infrequent itemset is immediately pruned (red, dashed) — dramatically reducing the search space without missing any valid frequent itemset.

(b) Data Preparation

ARM requires unlabeled binary transaction data. Each patient is a transaction; each symptom is either present or absent. The class label is removed entirely. Ordinal features (0–3) are binarised: score ≥ 2 is treated as "symptom present" — a clinically motivated threshold for moderate-to-severe presentation. Scores of 0–1 (mild or absent) are treated as absent.

01
Remove class label
ARM is fully unsupervised — no disease label is included in any form
02
Binarise at threshold ≥ 2
Score 0–1 → absent (0). Score 2–3 → present (1). Clinically meaningful: moderate-to-severe symptom presence
03
Export transaction matrix
Saved as arm_transactions.csv — 366 rows × 34 binary symptom indicators
# Binarise all features at moderate severity threshold df_arm_bin = df.drop(columns=['class']).applymap( lambda x: 1 if x >= 2 else 0 ) from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules frequent_itemsets = apriori(df_arm_bin.astype(bool), min_support=0.20, use_colnames=True) rules = association_rules(frequent_itemsets, metric='confidence', min_threshold=0.50)

(c) Results — Top Rules

Thresholds used: min_support = 0.20 (pattern present in ≥ 20% of patients), min_confidence = 0.50 (consequent present in ≥ 50% of antecedent cases). Rules are ranked by lift to surface the most informative non-obvious associations.

(e) Conclusions

ARM revealed several clinically meaningful symptom co-occurrence patterns without using any disease labels. The strongest associations by lift were concentrated among histopathological rete ridge features — clubbing, elongation, and thinning appearing together as a tight triad that ARM recovered entirely from data structure. This triad is the established hallmark of psoriasis.

A separate cluster of high-lift rules connected follicular features (follicular papules, perifollicular parakeratosis, follicular horn plug) — the histological signature of Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris. ARM independently confirmed that these symptoms form a coherent complex corresponding to a known diagnostic criterion.

The highest-support rules confirmed that erythema and acanthosis co-occur in nearly half of all patients — a direct statistical reflection of why these six conditions are grouped together as erythemato-squamous diseases, and why surface clinical signs alone remain unreliable for differential diagnosis.

Module 3 · Supervised Learning

Decision Tree Classification

Decision Trees learn a hierarchy of if–then rules from labeled training data, producing transparent, human-readable classifiers that mirror clinical reasoning — achieving 93% accuracy on this dermatology dataset.

(a) Overview

A Decision Tree recursively partitions the feature space into regions, each associated with a class prediction. At each internal node, the algorithm selects the feature and threshold that best separates the classes; leaf nodes contain the final predictions. Because the resulting structure is a tree of human-readable rules, DTs are among the most interpretable models in machine learning — a clinician can trace the exact path from symptoms to diagnosis.

Decision Tree — Structure

A schematic of how a DT partitions the feature space. Each internal node tests one feature against a threshold; each leaf predicts a disease class. The path from root to leaf is an explicit diagnostic rule.

Gini, Entropy & Information Gain

Both Gini impurity and Entropy measure class mixing in a node. Gini = 1 − Σ pᵢ²; Entropy = −Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ). Information Gain quantifies how much a split reduces impurity — the algorithm greedily picks the split with the highest IG at every node.

Why can infinitely many trees exist? At each node, any feature can be chosen and any threshold value along its range is a valid split point. With 34 features and continuous thresholds, the number of possible splits at each node is effectively infinite. Additionally, trees can grow to arbitrary depth, and the same data can be split in different orders, producing different tree topologies with equal or near-equal training accuracy. This is why regularisation through depth limits and minimum-sample thresholds is necessary.

The diagram below works through a concrete numerical example — a 24-patient parent node with three classes (A=10, B=10, C=4) — calculating Gini impurity, Entropy, and Information Gain for a split, then comparing IG across three candidate splits to show how the algorithm picks the best one.

Worked Example — Gini, Entropy & Information Gain

Left: Gini before and after split (IG = 0.455). Centre: Entropy for the same split (IG = 1.142). Right: IG comparison across three candidate splits — the DT always picks the split with the highest Information Gain.

(b) Data Preparation

The same stratified 80/20 split used for NB (292 train / 74 test) was applied here. Decision Trees natively handle ordinal integer features without scaling — no StandardScaler is needed. Three distinct trees are built with different hyperparameters to demonstrate how root node and depth choices affect the decision boundary.

Load df_saved.csv — same X/y split as NB
34 ordinal features (0–3) + continuous age; target y ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}
02
Stratified 80/20 split (same seed as NB for fair comparison)
train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
03
Tree 1 — Gini criterion, no max_depth (default)
Fully grown tree; highest complexity, best training fit
04
Tree 2 — Entropy criterion, max_depth = 4
Entropy-based splitting; moderate pruning to prevent overfitting
05
Tree 3 — Gini criterion, max_depth = 3 (shallow / interpretable)
Most constrained tree; highest interpretability, lowest variance

Tree 2: Entropy depth=4 — 86.49%

10 errors. Limiting depth to 4 hurts: Class 6 (all 4 test cases misclassified as Class 2) shows the tree hasn't learned the follicular features that define PRP within 4 split levels.

Tree 3: Gini depth=3 — 77.03%

17 errors. At depth 3, the tree collapses all Class 4 (Pityriasis Rosea) test cases into Class 2 — confirming that distinguishing these two conditions requires more than three feature splits.

Depth vs Accuracy Tradeoff

Visual Tree Snapshots

Each of the three trained trees is shown below as a full visual structure. The colour of each node represents the majority class; darker shades indicate higher purity. These snapshots make the if–then rule structure explicit and human-readable.

Tree 1 — Gini (Full Depth, first 3 levels shown)

The fully grown tree reaches depth 14 with 57 leaf nodes. The first split always uses thinning_suprapapillary_epidermis — the single most discriminating histopathological feature. Only the first 3 levels are shown here for readability; the full tree is available in the notebook.

Tree 2 — Entropy Criterion, max_depth = 4

Limited to 4 levels, producing 13 leaf nodes. Entropy-based splitting selects a different root split than Gini. At this depth, Class 6 (PRP) is completely absorbed into Class 2 — confirming that its rare follicular signature requires deeper branching to distinguish.

Tree 3 — Gini Criterion, max_depth = 3 (fully shown)

The shallowest tree — only 3 levels, 8 leaf nodes — is fully rendered here. Every split and leaf label is readable. The root splits on thinning_suprapapillary_epidermis, followed by follicular_papules and clubbing_rete_ridges. Despite its simplicity, this tree achieves 77% accuracy.

(e) Conclusions

The full Gini tree (93.24%) outperforms depth-limited variants, demonstrating that the dermatology feature space requires several levels of nesting to fully separate all six classes. The clear accuracy cliff between depth=3 (77%) and full depth (93%) shows that early splits cannot resolve the most clinically ambiguous pairs — Classes 2 and 4, and Class 6 — without deeper branching.

Decision Trees offer a unique advantage for clinical deployment: the rules they learn are human-readable. A dermatologist can trace through the tree's logic and validate whether each split corresponds to known clinical knowledge. Notably, the first splits in the trained trees consistently involve histopathological features (thinning suprapapillary epidermis, clubbing rete ridges) — the exact features that pathologists examine when differentiating these conditions, providing a valuable layer of model trustworthiness.

Module 3 · Supervised Learning

Naïve Bayes Classification

Naïve Bayes applies Bayes' theorem with a "naïve" assumption of feature independence to probabilistically classify patients — achieving 94–96% accuracy on the dermatology dataset across three flavours.

(a) Overview

Naïve Bayes is a family of probabilistic classifiers built on Bayes' theorem: P(class | features) ∝ P(features | class) × P(class). The "naïve" assumption is that features are conditionally independent given the class label — a simplification that rarely holds strictly in real data but enables fast, closed-form learning that performs surprisingly well in high-dimensional settings. NB has two main strengths: it is extremely sample-efficient (it learns useful models even with small training sets) and it naturally outputs calibrated probabilities rather than just hard labels.

There are four main sklearn NB variants, each suited to different data distributions:

VariantData typeHow it models P(features|class)When to use
Multinomial NB Non-negative counts / ordinal Multinomial distribution over counts. Probability proportional to feature frequency in each class. Text (word counts), ordinal symptom scores (our dataset). Requires non-negative features.
Gaussian NB Continuous (any sign) Assumes each feature follows a Gaussian (normal) distribution per class. Estimates mean and variance per feature per class. Truly continuous data — sensor readings, measurements. Works with negative values. Most flexible.
Bernoulli NB Binary (0/1) Models presence/absence of each feature. Penalises both non-occurrence and occurrence independently. Binary data — e.g. symptom present/absent. Must binarise ordinal features first. Often stronger than Multinomial for sparse binary data.
Categorical NB Ordinal / nominal integers Fits a separate categorical distribution per feature per class. Treats each ordinal value (0,1,2,3) as a distinct category. Ordinal features with a fixed, discrete value set. Ideal for this dataset but sensitive to unseen values.

Smoothing in Naïve Bayes

A critical practical issue in Naïve Bayes is the zero-probability problem: if a particular feature value never appears in the training set for a given class, its estimated probability is exactly zero — which then zeroes out the entire posterior probability, no matter how strong the other evidence is. Laplace smoothing (also called additive smoothing) solves this by adding a small constant α to every count before computing probabilities. The smoothed estimate becomes:

P(xᵢ = v | y = c) = (N(xᵢ=v, y=c) + α) / (N(y=c) + α × |V|)

With α = 1 (Laplace smoothing), no probability ever becomes exactly zero — every feature value gets at least a small positive probability in every class. In sklearn, MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) and BernoulliNB(alpha=1.0) both use Laplace smoothing by default. GaussianNB uses a different mechanism: var_smoothing, which adds a small fraction of the largest variance to all computed variances to prevent numerical instability.

Laplace (Additive) Smoothing — Concept & Formula

Without smoothing (α=0), a single unseen feature value collapses the entire posterior to zero. Laplace smoothing (α=1) ensures every probability stays positive. The formula above shows how each count is inflated by α before dividing by the adjusted total.

For this dermatology dataset, Multinomial NB is a natural fit because all features are non-negative ordinal scores (0–3). Gaussian NB treats these scores as continuous real-valued measurements. Bernoulli NB binarises each feature (score ≥ 1 = present) and models presence/absence — capturing a clinically meaningful threshold. All three are run and compared below.

(b) Data Preparation

Supervised learning requires labeled data split into disjoint Training and Testing sets. The cleaned dataset (df_saved.csv, 366 × 35) was used with the class column as the label and the remaining 34 features as predictors. An 80/20 stratified split was applied — stratified to preserve each class's proportion in both sets.

292Training rows (80%)
74Testing rows (20%)
34Feature columns
6Target classes

Why must Train and Test be disjoint? The model must never "see" the test examples during training. If even one test record leaks into training, the accuracy estimate becomes optimistically biased — the model has partially memorised its exam. Stratification ensures each disease class occupies the same proportion in both splits, preventing a scenario where a rare class (e.g. Class 6 with only 20 patients) is entirely absent from one set.

(e) Conclusions

All three NB variants achieve strong accuracy (86–96%) on the dermatology classification task, confirming that symptom features carry high diagnostic signal even under the independence assumption. Bernoulli NB (95.95%) outperforms both alternatives — binarising at score ≥ 1 (any symptom presence) turns out to be the most informative representation for this dataset. Multinomial NB (94.59%) is close behind, leveraging the full ordinal counts. Gaussian NB (86.49%) performs worst because the Gaussian distribution is a poor fit for discrete ordinal scores concentrated at integers 0–3.

The consistent pattern across all three matrices — Class 2 (Seborrheic Dermatitis) being confused with Class 4 (Pityriasis Rosea) — mirrors both clinical reality and our earlier clustering results: these two diseases genuinely overlap in their feature profiles, and no probabilistic model trained on this feature set fully resolves the ambiguity. A clinician facing this situation would reach for additional biopsy markers not in this dataset.

Module 4 · Supervised Learning

Support Vector Machine (SVM)

SVMs find the widest possible margin between classes — transforming complex clinical data into linearly separable problems through kernels, achieving up to 95.95% accuracy on the dermatology dataset.

(a) Overview

A Support Vector Machine is a supervised classifier that finds a hyperplane (a decision boundary) that maximally separates two classes in the feature space. Unlike other classifiers that merely seek any boundary that works, SVMs specifically maximise the margin — the perpendicular distance between the boundary and the nearest training points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors, and they alone define the boundary. This maximum-margin approach makes SVMs resistant to noise and strong generalisers.

SVMs are fundamentally linear separators — they draw a straight hyperplane in some feature space. The genius of the kernel trick is that it allows SVMs to implicitly work in a much higher-dimensional feature space without ever computing coordinates there. The dot product between two points — the core operation in every SVM computation — can be replaced by a kernel function K(x, z) that computes what the dot product would be in the higher-dimensional space, cheaply and exactly. This is why the dot product is so critical: the entire SVM optimisation and prediction can be expressed purely in terms of dot products between training points, making the kernel substitution possible.

SVM Maximum Margin (left) and Kernel Trick (right)

Left: the SVM finds the hyperplane that maximises the margin between classes; support vectors (circled) define it. Right: the kernel trick maps non-separable 1D data to a 2D space where a linear separator works perfectly — without ever explicitly computing the transformation.

Polynomial Kernel Casting, RBF Shape, and Polynomial Shape

Left: a 2D point (x₁,x₂) cast into 6D via the polynomial kernel with r=1, d=2. Centre: RBF kernel values vs distance for different γ. Right: polynomial kernel shape for degrees 2–4.

Kernel Functions

KernelFormulaParametersWhen to use
LinearK(x,z) = x·zNoneLinearly separable data, many features, text classification
PolynomialK(x,z) = (x·z + r)^dr (offset), d (degree)Feature interactions matter; moderate nonlinearity
RBF / GaussianK(x,z) = exp(−γ||x−z||²)γ (bandwidth)General-purpose; works well on most tabular datasets

Polynomial Casting Example — 2D → 6D

With a polynomial kernel K(x,z) = (x·z + 1)² (r=1, d=2), a 2D point (x₁, x₂) is implicitly cast into 6 dimensions via the mapping φ(x) = (x₁², x₂², √2·x₁x₂, √2·x₁, √2·x₂, 1). For the concrete example point (2, 3): φ(2,3) = (4, 9, 6√2, 2√2, 3√2, 1) ≈ (4, 9, 8.49, 2.83, 4.24, 1). The inner product of two such 6D vectors equals the kernel value computed directly in 2D — this is the kernel trick in action.

(b) Data Preparation

SVMs require labeled numeric data. This is because the SVM optimisation problem involves computing dot products and distances between feature vectors — operations only defined for numbers. Categorical text labels would make distance computations meaningless. Only the labeled class column provides the supervision signal; all 34 feature columns must be numeric (our dermatology dataset satisfies both requirements). Additionally, SVMs are highly sensitive to feature scale — features with large ranges dominate the margin computation — so StandardScaler normalisation is essential before fitting.

Why must Train and Test be disjoint? The SVM learns support vectors from training data only. If any test patient appeared in training, the model would have already "seen" their label, inflating accuracy estimates. StandardScaler is also fit on training data only and then applied to the test set — preventing test-set statistics from influencing normalisation.

(e) Conclusions

The RBF kernel (C=10) is the best SVM configuration at 95.95% accuracy — matching the top performers from all previous modules. Its ability to model smooth, curved boundaries in high-dimensional space suits the ordinal dermatology features better than the linear or polynomial alternatives. The linear kernel (93.24%) is competitive and interpretable. The polynomial kernel (89.19%) underperforms, likely because its rigid degree-3 boundary structure does not naturally fit the correlation patterns in this dataset.

The persistent Class 2 vs 4 confusion — Seborrheic Dermatitis misclassified as Pityriasis Rosea — appears across all three SVM kernels, consistent with every other model in this project. No kernel removes this ambiguity, further confirming it is a genuine data-level challenge rather than a modelling limitation. SVMs are a strong choice for clinical deployment because they naturally output a confidence margin — how far a test patient falls from the decision boundary — which clinicians can use to flag borderline cases for additional testing.

Module 3 · Supervised Learning

Regression Analysis

Logistic Regression applies a sigmoid-transformed linear model to produce class probabilities, achieving 95.95% accuracy — tied with Bernoulli NB as the top performer among all three Module 3 models.

(a) Linear Regression

Linear regression models the relationship between one or more continuous input features and a continuous numeric output using a weighted sum: ŷ = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + … + βₙxₙ. The coefficients (β) are estimated by minimising the sum of squared residuals between predicted and actual values. The output is a real number, making linear regression appropriate for predicting quantities such as patient age, biomarker concentration, or severity score — not class labels.

(b) Logistic Regression

Logistic regression models the probability that an observation belongs to a particular class. It applies the sigmoid (logistic) function to a linear combination of features, squashing the output to the range (0, 1): P(y=1|X) = σ(β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + βₙxₙ) = 1 / (1 + e^−z). For multi-class problems like ours (six disease classes), a one-vs-rest (OvR) strategy trains one binary classifier per class. Despite the name, logistic regression is a classification model, not a regression model for continuous outputs.

(c) Similarities and Differences

Both methods use a linear combination of input features and share a coefficient-based interpretation — each β weight indicates the direction and magnitude of a feature's contribution. The critical difference is the output: linear regression predicts a real-valued continuous number, while logistic regression predicts a probability (via sigmoid) and thresholds it into a discrete class label. Linear regression minimises squared error (MSE); logistic regression minimises log-loss (cross-entropy), which is the appropriate loss for probability estimation tasks.

(d) Does logistic regression use the Sigmoid function?

Yes, absolutely. The sigmoid function σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) is what makes logistic regression "logistic." It maps any real-valued linear score z to a probability between 0 and 1. Without the sigmoid, the output could be any real number — impossible to interpret as a probability. For multi-class settings, a softmax generalisation of sigmoid is often used (multinomial logistic regression), which produces a probability distribution over all classes that sums to 1.

(e) Maximum Likelihood and Logistic Regression

Logistic regression is estimated by Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE). The likelihood function measures how probable the observed training labels are under the current model parameters. The algorithm finds the coefficients β that maximise this likelihood — equivalently, it minimises the negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy loss). Unlike linear regression's closed-form OLS solution, MLE for logistic regression has no closed form and is solved iteratively via gradient descent or Newton-Raphson. This connection to MLE gives logistic regression principled uncertainty estimates and well-calibrated probabilities, unlike most other classifiers.

The Sigmoid Function

Maps any real-valued linear score z to a probability between 0 and 1. At z=0 the predicted probability is exactly 0.5 — the decision boundary. Increasing z pushes the output toward 1 (positive class); decreasing z pushes toward 0.

Conclusions

Logistic Regression achieves the highest test accuracy on this dermatology classification task, tied with Bernoulli NB at 95.95%. The remaining 3 errors are concentrated in the clinically hardest pair — Class 2 (Seborrheic Dermatitis) vs Class 4 (Pityriasis Rosea) — a finding consistent across every model in this module and echoed by the clustering and ARM analyses in Module 2. No supervised model in this study fully resolves this ambiguity, suggesting that the 34 available features are insufficient to perfectly separate these two conditions without additional diagnostic markers.

The progression from linear to logistic regression illustrates a fundamental principle: the correct choice of output function matters as much as the choice of features. A linear regression applied to this problem would produce meaningless real-valued predictions (e.g. "2.73") that cannot be interpreted as class labels. The sigmoid-transformed logistic model produces interpretable probabilities directly usable in clinical decision support — highlighting that model design must always be driven by the nature of the target variable, not just by convenience.

Module 4 · Ensemble Learning

Ensemble Learning — Random Forest

Random Forest combines hundreds of decision trees into a single powerful classifier — achieving 93.24% accuracy on the dermatology dataset while revealing which clinical features matter most for diagnosis.

(a) What is Ensemble Learning?

Ensemble learning combines multiple individual models ("weak learners") into a single, stronger predictor. The core idea is that a committee of diverse models, each making different errors, collectively outperforms any single member. The main ensemble strategies are:

StrategyHow it worksExamples
BaggingTrain many models on different random bootstrap samples of the data; combine by majority vote or averaging. Reduces variance.Random Forest
BoostingTrain models sequentially; each new model focuses on the mistakes of the previous ones. Reduces bias.AdaBoost, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting
StackingTrain a "meta-model" to learn the best way to combine predictions from multiple base models.StackingClassifier
VotingCombine predictions from different model types by majority vote (hard) or probability averaging (soft).VotingClassifier

Random Forest — Architecture

Random Forest is a bagging method that trains a large collection of decision trees, each on a different bootstrap sample of the training data and using a random subset of features at each split. This double randomness — in both data samples and feature subsets — ensures the trees are diverse and decorrelated, dramatically reducing overfitting compared to a single deep decision tree. Predictions are made by majority vote across all trees.

Random Forest Architecture (left) and Top 12 Feature Importances (right)

Left: each bootstrap sample feeds an independent tree; all trees vote to produce the final prediction. Right: the Random Forest assigns importance scores to each feature based on how much each split using that feature reduces Gini impurity across all 200 trees. Histopathological rete-ridge features dominate — consistent with clinical knowledge.

Conclusions

Random Forest achieves 94.59% accuracy — competitive, reliable, and highly interpretable through its feature importance scores. Sitting just below the top performers (RBF SVM, Bernoulli NB, and Logistic Regression at 95.95%), it provides a critical additional insight: the ranked importance of every clinical feature. The consistent top features across all tree-based methods — thinning suprapapillary epidermis, clubbing rete ridges, elongation rete ridges — are exactly the histopathological criteria pathologists use in manual diagnosis. This agreement between computational results and clinical knowledge is the strongest validation this project produces.

Random Forest also offers practical advantages for clinical deployment: it is robust to outliers and missing values, requires no feature scaling, naturally handles the multi-class problem, and provides out-of-bag error estimates. For a hospital system that needs a reliable, explainable, and low-maintenance classifier, Random Forest is an excellent choice even when its raw accuracy sits just below the theoretical maximum.

Module 4 · Final Conclusions

Conclusions

After applying ten distinct analytical methods to 366 dermatology patients, one story emerges with remarkable consistency: the right computational tools can match and support expert clinical diagnosis — and the data itself reveals truths that align with decades of medical knowledge.

The Complete Data Science Journey — From Raw Data to Clinical Insight

Seven stages of analysis from data preparation through ensemble learning. Each stage built on the previous, uncovering deeper patterns. The key finding — that thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis and clubbing of rete ridges are the most discriminating features — emerged independently from PCA, clustering, ARM, decision trees, and Random Forest.

What We Discovered

This project began with a simple but important question: can a computer, given clinical and biopsy information from a patient's skin, correctly identify which of six closely related skin diseases they have? The short answer is yes — with accuracy consistently above 93%, and rising to nearly 96% with the best methods. To put that in perspective: dermatologists examining the same cases, without the full set of 34 features, often face genuine diagnostic uncertainty between the most similar conditions. The computational models in this project had access to every recorded feature simultaneously, allowing them to catch patterns that might be missed by focusing on any single clinical sign.

The single most important discovery is not a number — it is a confirmation. Every analytical method applied here, from the earliest unsupervised clustering to the final Random Forest, pointed to the same two histopathological features as the strongest diagnostic signals: thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis and clubbing of the rete ridges. These are precisely the features pathologists examine most carefully when distinguishing psoriasis from other erythemato-squamous diseases. The fact that a machine learning algorithm, given no medical knowledge, independently discovered the same features through pure data analysis is a powerful validation of both the dataset and the methodology.

One challenge appeared in every single model without exception: the boundary between Seborrheic Dermatitis (Class 2) and Pityriasis Rosea (Class 4). No method — not Naïve Bayes, not Decision Trees, not SVMs, not Logistic Regression, not even the Random Forest — could perfectly separate these two conditions. This is not a failure of the models; it is a genuine reflection of clinical reality. These two diseases share overlapping presentations, and even experienced dermatologists sometimes require repeat biopsies or treatment response monitoring to distinguish them. The consistent 2–3 errors between these classes across all models is actually a meaningful finding: it tells us that the 34 features in this dataset, however rich, are not sufficient alone to fully resolve this specific diagnostic pair.

What the Numbers Mean

Across all the methods applied in this project, accuracy ranged from 77% (the most constrained Decision Tree) to 96% (the RBF SVM, Bernoulli Naïve Bayes, and Logistic Regression — all tied at 95.95%). Rather than chasing the last decimal point, the more important insight is why different methods perform differently. The simple Decision Tree with only three levels of branching loses information about rare conditions because it runs out of splits before reaching the nuanced combinations of features that define unusual presentations. The RBF SVM, by contrast, creates smooth curved boundaries that naturally handle the gradual overlaps in symptom severity scores. Naïve Bayes surprises by performing equally well despite its strong simplifying assumptions — a reminder that elegant mathematical foundations can be remarkably effective in practice.

Final Model Rankings — All 10 Methods, Ordered by Accuracy

The top cluster (Bernoulli NB, Logistic Regression, RBF SVM — all at 95.95%) represents the ceiling achievable with this feature set. Random Forest lands at 94.59%. The gap between 95% and 100% is attributable to the genuine Class 2 vs Class 4 ambiguity present in the data itself, not a modelling failure.

What This Means for Patients

The practical implication of this work is straightforward: a well-designed machine learning classifier, trained on structured clinical and biopsy data, can serve as a reliable second opinion in dermatological diagnosis. For the five conditions it classifies near-perfectly (Psoriasis, Lichen Planus, Pityriasis Rosea as a clean detection, Chronic Dermatitis, and Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris), the model could reduce diagnostic delays, lower the need for repeat biopsies, and give rural or under-resourced clinicians access to specialist-level diagnostic support. For the hard case — the Seborrheic Dermatitis vs. Pityriasis Rosea distinction — the model is honest about its uncertainty in a way that human overconfidence sometimes is not, flagging borderline cases for additional clinical attention rather than forcing a wrong answer.

The Bigger Picture

This project demonstrated the full data science lifecycle from start to finish: data collection and cleaning, exploratory visualisation, dimensionality reduction, unsupervised pattern discovery, association mining, and finally a progression of supervised classification methods each illuminating a different aspect of the same problem. No single method told the whole story; the richest insights came from comparing and triangulating across approaches. That is the core lesson of applied data science — not "which algorithm is best" but "what does the convergence of multiple methods reveal about the underlying reality?" In this case, the answer is a scientifically grounded, clinically meaningful, and technically rigorous understanding of what makes these six skin diseases distinct — and where the boundaries genuinely blur.
